Problem Statement¶

Business Context¶

A sales forecast is a prediction of future sales revenue based on historical data, industry trends, and the status of the current sales pipeline. Businesses use the sales forecast to estimate weekly, monthly, quarterly, and annual sales totals. A company needs to make an accurate sales forecast as it adds value across an organization and helps the different verticals to chalk out their future course of action.

Forecasting helps an organization plan its sales operations by region and provides valuable insights to the supply chain team regarding the procurement of goods and materials. An accurate sales forecast process has many benefits which include improved decision-making about the future and reduction of sales pipeline and forecast risks. Moreover, it helps to reduce the time spent in planning territory coverage and establish benchmarks that can be used to assess trends in the future.

Objective¶

SuperKart is a retail chain operating supermarkets and food marts across various tier cities, offering a wide range of products. To optimize its inventory management and make informed decisions around regional sales strategies, SuperKart wants to accurately forecast the sales revenue of its outlets for the upcoming quarter.

To operationalize these insights at scale, the company has partnered with a data science firm—not just to build a predictive model based on historical sales data, but to develop and deploy a robust forecasting solution that can be integrated into SuperKart’s decision-making systems and used across its network of stores.

Data Description¶

The data contains the different attributes of the various products and stores.The detailed data dictionary is given below.

  • Product_Id - unique identifier of each product, each identifier having two letters at the beginning followed by a number.
  • Product_Weight - weight of each product
  • Product_Sugar_Content - sugar content of each product like low sugar, regular and no sugar
  • Product_Allocated_Area - ratio of the allocated display area of each product to the total display area of all the products in a store
  • Product_Type - broad category for each product like meat, snack foods, hard drinks, dairy, canned, soft drinks, health and hygiene, baking goods, bread, breakfast, frozen foods, fruits and vegetables, household, seafood, starchy foods, others
  • Product_MRP - maximum retail price of each product
  • Store_Id - unique identifier of each store
  • Store_Establishment_Year - year in which the store was established
  • Store_Size - size of the store depending on sq. feet like high, medium and low
  • Store_Location_City_Type - type of city in which the store is located like Tier 1, Tier 2 and Tier 3. Tier 1 consists of cities where the standard of living is comparatively higher than its Tier 2 and Tier 3 counterparts.
  • Store_Type - type of store depending on the products that are being sold there like Departmental Store, Supermarket Type 1, Supermarket Type 2 and Food Mart
  • Product_Store_Sales_Total - total revenue generated by the sale of that particular product in that particular store

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Function to do Count Plot for all CATEGORICAL variables
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

def plot_categorical(
    data: pd.DataFrame,
    column: str,
    hue: str | None = None,
    palette: str = "Set2",
    order: list | None = None,
    top_n: int | None = None,
    rotate_xticks: int = 0,
    figsize: tuple = (10, 7),
):
    """
    Count Plot for a categorical column.

    Parameters
    ----------
    data         : DataFrame
    column       : Categorical column to plot
    hue          : Optional target column to split bars by
    palette      : Seaborn palette
    order        : Explicit category order (overrides top_n)
    top_n        : Show only the top-N most frequent categories
    rotate_xticks: Rotate x-axis labels by this many degrees
    figsize      : (width, height)
    """
    plot_data = data[[column] + ([hue] if hue else [])].dropna()
    total     = len(plot_data)

    # ── Resolve bar order ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
    value_counts = plot_data[column].value_counts()
    if order is not None:
        plot_order = order
    elif top_n is not None:
        plot_order = value_counts.head(top_n).index.tolist()
    else:
        plot_order = value_counts.index.tolist()

    # ── Count Plot ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=figsize)
    sns.countplot(
        data=plot_data[plot_data[column].isin(plot_order)],
        x=column, order=plot_order,
        hue=hue, palette=palette, ax=ax,
    )
    ax.set_title(
        f"Count Plot of '{column}'" + (f"  |  by '{hue}'" if hue else ""),
        fontsize=11, fontweight="bold",
    )
    ax.set_xlabel(column)
    ax.set_ylabel("Count")
    ax.tick_params(axis="x", rotation=rotate_xticks)

    # ── Bar labels: count + % (per bar when no hue; count only with hue) ──
    for p in ax.patches:
        h = int(p.get_height())
        if h == 0:
            continue
        label = f"{h}\n({h/total*100:.1f}%)" if not hue else f"{h}"
        ax.annotate(
            label,
            (p.get_x() + p.get_width() / 2.0, h),
            ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=9, linespacing=1.4,
        )

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

    # ── Frequency table ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    print(f"\n── '{column}' value counts ──")
    if hue:
        print(plot_data.groupby([column, hue]).size().unstack(fill_value=0).to_string())
    else:
        freq = (
            value_counts[plot_order]
            .reset_index(name="Count")
            .rename(columns={"index": column})
            .assign(Pct=lambda df: (df["Count"] / total * 100).round(1))
        )
        print(freq.to_string(index=False))

Detailed Observations on Categorical Variables:¶

  • Product_Sugar_Content:
    • Low Sugar dominates the dataset, constituting the largest share at approximately 55.7% (4,885 products).
    • Regular Sugar content represents the second most prevalent category at 25.7% (2,359 products).
    • No Sugar items represent 17.3% of the selection (1,519 products).
    • A minor labeling discrepancy exists where 1.2% of items (108 products) are annotated as 'reg' instead of 'Regular', pointing to a data cleaning requirement.
  • Product_Type:
    • Fruits and Vegetables (14.3%) and Snack Foods (13.1%) are the primary driver categories, collectively representing more than a quarter of all inventory.
    • Core staple categories including Frozen Foods (9.3%), Dairy (9.1%), Household (8.4%), Baking Goods (8.2%), and Canned products (7.7%) maintain stable, moderate representation.
    • Niche or premium categories such as Breakfast (1.2%) and Seafood (0.9%) represent minimal shares of the total product catalog.
  • Store_Id:
    • Store OUT004 alone accounts for 53.4% (4,676 records) of all observations, representing a significant skew in transaction volume or reporting activity.
    • The remaining records are distributed relatively evenly among OUT001 (18.1%), OUT003 (15.4%), and OUT002 (13.1%).
  • Store Demographics (Size, Location, Type):
    • Size: Medium-sized stores represent the vast majority at 68.8%, while High-sized stores account for 18.1%, and Small-sized stores account for 13.1%.
    • City Tier: Stores in Tier 2 cities hold the dominant share at 71.5%, far exceeding Tier 1 (15.4%) and Tier 3 (13.1%) representation.
    • Store Type: Supermarket Type 2 is the most prominent model, housing 53.4% of the data, followed by Supermarket Type 1 (18.1%), Departmental Stores (15.4%), and Food Marts (13.1%). This distribution aligns precisely with the respective Store IDs (e.g., OUT004 represents Supermarket Type 2, Medium, Tier 2).

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Function to do  Histogram  +  Box Plot for all  NUMERICAL columns
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

def plot_numerical(
    data: pd.DataFrame,
    column: str,
    hue: str | None = None,
    bins: int = 30,
    color: str = "steelblue",
    palette: str = "Set2",
    kde: bool = False,
    figsize: tuple = (12, 4),
):
    """
    Histogram + Box Plot for a numerical column.

    Parameters
    ----------
    data    : DataFrame
    column  : Numerical column to plot
    hue     : Optional target column to split/colour plots by
    bins    : Histogram bin count
    color   : Bar colour when hue is None
    palette : Seaborn palette when hue is set
    kde     : Overlay KDE curve on histogram
    figsize : (width, height)
    """
    plot_data = data[[column] + ([hue] if hue else [])].dropna()

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=figsize)
    fig.suptitle(
        f"Distribution of '{column}'" + (f"  |  by '{hue}'" if hue else ""),
        fontsize=13, fontweight="bold",
    )

    # ── Histogram ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    sns.histplot(
        data=plot_data, x=column,
        hue=hue, bins=bins, kde=kde,
        palette=palette if hue else None,
        color=color if not hue else None,
        edgecolor="white", ax=axes[0],
    )
    axes[0].set_title(f"Histogram{'  + KDE' if kde else ''}")
    skew_val = plot_data[column].skew()
    axes[0].text(
        0.97, 0.95, f"Skew: {skew_val:.2f}",
        transform=axes[0].transAxes, ha="right", va="top", fontsize=9,
        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.3", facecolor="lightyellow", alpha=0.8),
    )

    # ── Box Plot ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    sns.boxplot(
        data=plot_data, x=hue, y=column,
        hue=hue, palette=palette if hue else None,
        color=color if not hue else None,
        legend=False, ax=axes[1],
    )
    axes[1].set_title("Box Plot")
    axes[1].set_xlabel(hue or "")

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

    # ── Summary stats ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    print(f"\n── '{column}' summary ──")
    if hue:
        print(plot_data.groupby(hue)[column].describe().round(2).to_string())
    else:
        print(plot_data[column].describe().round(2).to_string())

Detailed Observations on Numerical Variables:¶

  • Product_Weight:
    • The distribution is highly symmetric and near-uniform across the range of 4.00 to 22.00, with a mean of 12.65 and a median of 12.66.
    • A skewness metric of 0.02 confirms an almost perfectly balanced distribution, with no significant structural outliers or heavy tails in either direction.
  • Product_Allocated_Area:
    • Highly right-skewed with a skewness coefficient of 1.13, reflecting typical retail shelf space constraints.
    • The average space allocated per product is small at 6.88% (median 5.60%), with the bulk of inventory restricted to under 10% display area.
    • A maximum allocation of 29.8% exists, indicating a few high-profile promotional items.
  • Product_MRP:
    • Maximum Retail Price ranges from 31.00 to 266.00 with an average price of 147.03 (median 146.74).
    • The distribution behaves in a relatively uniform and symmetric fashion (skewness of 0.04), indicating a diverse and balanced portfolio of low, mid, and high-value consumer goods.
  • Product_Store_Sales_Total (Target Variable):
    • The target variable spans from 33.00 up to a maximum of 8,000.00, indicating high variance in store performance.
    • Mean sales (3,464.00) are slightly higher than median sales (3,452.34), displaying a positive skew with tail events pointing to highly successful store-product combinations.

# ==============================================================================
# Bivariate Analysis (for Continuous Regression Target)
# ==============================================================================

def stacked_barplot(data, predictor, target):
    """
    Plots a 100% normalized stacked bar chart for two categorical variables.
    """
    tab = pd.crosstab(data[predictor], data[target], normalize="index") * 100
    ax = tab.plot(kind="bar", stacked=True, figsize=(10, 5), colormap="Set2")

    for p in ax.patches:
        width, height = p.get_width(), p.get_height()
        x, y = p.get_xy()
        if height > 5.0:
            ax.annotate(
                f'{height:.1f}%',
                (x + width / 2, y + height / 2),
                ha='center', va='center',
                color='black', fontweight='bold', fontsize=9
            )

    plt.legend(title=target, loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(1, 1))
    plt.ylabel("Percentage (%)")
    plt.xlabel(predictor)
    plt.title(f"Distribution of {target} by {predictor}", fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
    plt.xticks(rotation=45)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


def plot_bivariate_numeric(data, col_x, col_y, hue=None, figsize=(10, 5)):
    """
    Plots scatter distributions for numerical combinations or boxplots for mixed types.
    """
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=figsize)

    # Numerical vs Numerical -> Scatter Plot
    if pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(data[col_x]) and pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(data[col_y]):
        sns.scatterplot(data=data, x=col_x, y=col_y, hue=hue, palette="Set2", alpha=0.6, ax=ax)
        corr = data[[col_x, col_y]].corr().iloc[0, 1]
        ax.text(0.97, 0.05, f"r = {corr:.2f}", transform=ax.transAxes, ha="right", va="bottom",
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.3", facecolor="lightyellow", alpha=0.8))
        ax.set_title(f"Scatter: '{col_x}' vs '{col_y}'" + (f" | by '{hue}'" if hue else ""), fontweight='bold')

    # Categorical vs Numerical -> Clean Boxplot
    else:
        cat_c, num_c = (col_x, col_y) if not pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(data[col_x]) else (col_y, col_x)
        sns.boxplot(data=data, x=cat_c, y=num_c, hue=hue, palette="Set2", ax=ax)
        ax.set_title(f"Distribution of '{num_c}' across '{cat_c}'", fontweight='bold')
        plt.xticks(rotation=45)

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


def plot_bivariate_all(data, target, num_cols, cat_cols, extra_pairs=None):
    """
    Orchestrates the Bivariate Analysis phase in three clean passes.
    """
    # 1. Categorical Features vs Continuous Target -> Boxplots
    print("━" * 60)
    print(f" Categorical Features vs Target: '{target}'")
    print("━" * 60)
    for col in cat_cols:
        if col != target:
            plot_bivariate_numeric(data, col, target, hue=None)

    # 2. Numerical Features vs Continuous Target -> Scatterplots
    print("━" * 60)
    print(f" Numerical Features vs Target: '{target}'")
    print("━" * 60)
    for col in num_cols:
        if col != target:
            plot_bivariate_numeric(data, col, target, hue=None)

    # 3. Selected Feature-to-Feature Pairs
    if extra_pairs:
        print("━" * 60)
        print(" Selected Feature-to-Feature Pairs")
        print("━" * 60)
        for col_x, col_y in extra_pairs:
            if col_x in num_cols and col_y in num_cols:
                plot_bivariate_numeric(data, col_x, col_y, hue=None)
            elif col_x in num_cols or col_y in num_cols:
                plot_bivariate_numeric(data, col_x, col_y, hue=None)
            else:
                stacked_barplot(data, col_x, col_y)

Detailed Bivariate Analysis Observations:¶

Categorical vs. Target¶

  • Store Performance Analysis:
    • Store_Id: Outlets OUT003 and OUT001 show significantly stronger sales distributions, with median sales comfortably exceeding 4,000.00. In contrast, OUT004 (Supermarket Type 2) and OUT002 (Food Mart) show lower sales distributions (medians closer to 3,300.00 and 1,900.00 respectively).
    • Store_Size: Medium and High-sized outlets generate substantially higher median sales compared to Small-sized outlets, highlighting a strong relationship between store physical footprint and revenue generation.
    • Product_Type: Median sales remain consistent across different product types, showing that consumer demand profiles for essential categories (such as Dairy, Meat, and Produce) behave similarly when looking at overall sales totals.

Numerical vs. Target¶

  • MRP as a Primary Driver:
    • Product_MRP exhibits a strong, positive, linear-like upward bound with Product_Store_Sales_Total. Higher pricing bounds directly constrain the maximum revenue potential, showing that premium priced products are key contributors to high-value transactions.
  • No Strong Linear Associations:
    • Product_Weight shares virtually zero linear relationship with overall sales, showing that product physical weight does not dictate purchasing behavior or revenue outcomes.
    • Product_Allocated_Area displays a highly dispersed scatter plot relative to sales, demonstrating that increased display space does not guarantee higher store sales totals.

def plot_correlation(data, columns=None, method="pearson", cmap="coolwarm", figsize=(10, 8)):
    """
    Plots a clean, lower-triangle correlation heatmap for numerical columns.
    """
    num_data = data[columns] if columns else data.select_dtypes(include="number")
    num_data = num_data.dropna()
    corr_matrix = num_data.corr(method=method)

    mask = np.triu(np.ones_like(corr_matrix, dtype=bool))

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=figsize)
    sns.heatmap(
        corr_matrix, mask=mask, annot=True, fmt=".2f", cmap=cmap,
        vmin=-1, vmax=1, linewidths=0.5, square=True,
        annot_kws={"size": 10}, ax=ax
    )
    ax.set_title(f"Correlation Matrix ({method.capitalize()})", fontsize=13, fontweight="bold")
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


def plot_pairplot(data, columns, hue=None, palette="Set2", figsize=(12, 12)):
    """
    Plots a pairwise relationship grid across numerical features, optionally stratified by a categorical hue.
    """
    use_cols = columns + ([hue] if hue and hue not in columns else [])
    plot_data = data[use_cols].dropna()

    g = sns.pairplot(
        plot_data, vars=columns, hue=hue, palette=palette if hue else None,
        diag_kind="kde", kind="scatter",
        plot_kws={"alpha": 0.4, "s": 15},
        height=figsize[1] / len(columns)
    )
    g.figure.suptitle(f"Pair Plot" + (f" | by '{hue}'" if hue else ""), y=1.02, fontsize=13, fontweight="bold")
    plt.show()


def plot_multivariate_all(data, num_cols, hue_col=None):
    """
    Orchestrates the Multivariate Analysis phase.
    """
    print("━" * 60)
    print(" Numeric Feature Linear Correlations")
    print("━" * 60)
    plot_correlation(data, columns=num_cols)

    print("━" * 60)
    print(f" Pairwise Feature Interactions" + (f" Stratified by '{hue_col}'" if hue_col else ""))
    print("━" * 60)
    plot_pairplot(data, columns=num_cols, hue=hue_col)

Detailed Multivariate Analysis Observations:¶

  • Product_MRP and Sales Correlation:
    • A strong positive linear correlation of 0.79 is confirmed between Product_MRP and Product_Store_Sales_Total. This stable, high-value correlation persists across all store types, solidifying product pricing as the strongest predictive driver of store revenue.
  • Product_Weight and Sales Correlation:
    • A moderate-to-strong positive correlation of 0.74 is observed between Product_Weight and Product_Store_Sales_Total in the linear matrix, indicating that weight distributions may carry implicit categorizations (e.g., heavier items having distinct pricing scales or retail structures).
  • Product_Weight and MRP Interaction:
    • A moderate positive correlation of 0.53 exists between Product_Weight and Product_MRP, suggesting that bulkier or heavier packaging formats may systematically command higher retail pricing.
  • Year of Establishment Impact:
    • Store_Establishment_Year shows a weak negative correlation (-0.19) with overall sales. This suggests that longer-established stores (older years of establishment) retain slightly more robust or mature sales trends compared to newer outlets.

Data Preprocessing¶

From above Observations (for Data Preprocessing)¶

  • Data Completeness & Integrity: The dataset contains 8,763 records across 12 columns with zero missing values and zero duplicate entries, eliminating the need for missing-value imputation or deduplication.
  1. Categorical Label Standardization (Product_Sugar_Content): An inconsistent label ('reg', accounting for 1.23% or 108 records) refers to the same category as 'Regular' and requires standardization into a single 'Regular' class.
  2. Identifier Prefix Extraction (Product_Id $\rightarrow$ Product_Id_char): Raw Product_Id values have high cardinality and cannot be fed directly into regression models, but their two-letter prefixes (FD for Food, NC for Non-Consumables, DR for Drinks) capture structured domain information. Extracting Product_Id_char and dropping Product_Id retains signal while preventing overfitting.
  3. Temporal Feature Engineering (Store_Establishment_Year $\rightarrow$ Store_Age_Years): Converting the discrete establishment year (ranging from 1987 to 2009) into a continuous Store_Age_Years metric makes the temporal maturity of each outlet directly interpretable for linear and tree-based models.
  4. Category Consolidation (Product_Type $\rightarrow$ Product_Type_Category): Grouping the 16 granular Product_Type classes into broader supply-chain buckets (Perishables vs. Non-Perishables) reduces feature sparsity after one-hot encoding and aligns directly with inventory shelf-life planning.
  5. Redundant Identifier Removal (Store_Id): Store_Id (OUT001–OUT004) maps 1-to-1 with combinations of Store_Type, Store_Size, and Store_Location_City_Type, so dropping Store_Id prior to modeling avoids multicollinearity while allowing the model to generalize based on store characteristics.

Model Building¶

Define functions for Model Evaluation¶

In [35]:
# function to compute adjusted R-squared
def adj_r2_score(predictors, targets, predictions):
    r2 = r2_score(targets, predictions)
    n = predictors.shape[0]
    k = predictors.shape[1]
    return 1 - ((1 - r2) * (n - 1) / (n - k - 1))


# function to compute different metrics to check performance of a regression model
def model_performance_regression(model, predictors, target):
    """
    Function to compute different metrics to check regression model performance

    model: regressor
    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    """

    # predicting using the independent variables
    pred = model.predict(predictors)

    r2 = r2_score(target, pred)  # to compute R-squared
    adjr2 = adj_r2_score(predictors, target, pred)  # to compute adjusted R-squared
    rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(target, pred))  # to compute RMSE
    mae = mean_absolute_error(target, pred)  # to compute MAE
    mape = mean_absolute_percentage_error(target, pred)  # to compute MAPE

    # creating a dataframe of metrics
    df_perf = pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "RMSE": rmse,
            "MAE": mae,
            "R-squared": r2,
            "Adj. R-squared": adjr2,
            "MAPE": mape,
        },
        index=[0],
    )

    return df_perf

The ML models to be built can be any two out of the following:

  1. Decision Tree
  2. Bagging
  3. Random Forest
  4. AdaBoost
  5. Gradient Boosting
  6. XGBoost

Random Forest and XGBoost can be selected to evaluate two complementary ensemble architectures: parallel bagging (which minimizes variance across noisy retail transactions) versus sequential gradient boosting (which minimizes bias and uses regularization to prevent overfitting). Together, they excel at capturing complex, non-linear interactions between product pricing (Product_MRP) and categorical store formats (Store_Type, Store_Size) across a mixed numericals.

Observations:¶

  • Data Partitioning: The dataset is partitioned into 7,010 training records (80%) and 1,753 testing records (20%) across 10 predictive features, processed via StandardScaler for numerical variables and OneHotEncoder for categorical variables.
  • Baseline Random Forest Performance: Achieves a training $R^2$ of 0.9898 (RMSE: 107.53, MAE: 40.41, MAPE: 1.49%) and a testing $R^2$ of 0.9283 (RMSE: 286.12, MAE: 109.47, MAPE: 3.92%). The 6.15% drop in $R^2$ from training to testing indicates mild overfitting caused by unconstrained tree depth.
  • Baseline XGBoost Performance: Achieves a training $R^2$ of 0.9828 (RMSE: 139.70, MAE: 63.95, MAPE: 2.25%) and a testing $R^2$ of 0.9145 (RMSE: 312.28, MAE: 138.05, MAPE: 5.07%). Default boosting hyperparameters exhibit a 6.83% generalization gap between training and testing sets.
  • Baseline Comparison: Baseline Random Forest outperforms Baseline XGBoost across all test metrics, reducing test RMSE by 26.17 and test MAE by 28.58, while both models benefit from hyperparameter tuning to constrain tree complexity and improve out-of-sample generalization.

Model Performance Improvement - Hyperparameter Tuning¶

In [37]:
# ==============================================================================
# 1. Hyperparameter Tuning - Random Forest Regressor
# ==============================================================================
rf_tuned_pipeline = Pipeline([
    ("preprocessor", preprocessor),
    ("rf", RandomForestRegressor(random_state=42))
])

rf_param_grid = {
    "rf__n_estimators": [100, 200],
    "rf__max_depth": [6, 8, 10],
    "rf__max_features": [0.7, 1.0],
    "rf__min_samples_leaf": [2, 5]
}

rf_grid = GridSearchCV(
    estimator=rf_tuned_pipeline,
    param_grid=rf_param_grid,
    scoring="r2",
    cv=5,
    n_jobs=-1,
    verbose=1
)

rf_grid.fit(X_train, y_train)
rf_tuned_model = rf_grid.best_estimator_

print("Best Random Forest Parameters:", rf_grid.best_params_)
print("\n── Tuned Random Forest Performance ──")
rf_tuned_train_perf = model_performance_regression(rf_tuned_model, X_train, y_train)
rf_tuned_test_perf = model_performance_regression(rf_tuned_model, X_test, y_test)
print("Training Performance:")
display(rf_tuned_train_perf)
print("Testing Performance:")
display(rf_tuned_test_perf)

    ("preprocessor", preprocessor),

])

xgb_param_grid = {
    "xgb__n_estimators": [100, 150, 200],
    "xgb__max_depth": [3, 4, 5],
    "xgb__learning_rate": [0.05, 0.1],
    "xgb__subsample": [0.8, 1.0],
    "xgb__colsample_bytree": [0.8, 1.0]
}

xgb_grid = GridSearchCV(
    estimator=xgb_tuned_pipeline,
    param_grid=xgb_param_grid,
    scoring="r2",
    cv=5,
    n_jobs=-1,
    verbose=1
)

xgb_grid.fit(X_train, y_train)
xgb_tuned_model = xgb_grid.best_estimator_

print("Best XGBoost Parameters:", xgb_grid.best_params_)
print("\n── Tuned XGBoost Performance ──")
xgb_tuned_train_perf = model_performance_regression(xgb_tuned_model, X_train, y_train)
xgb_tuned_test_perf = model_performance_regression(xgb_tuned_model, X_test, y_test)
print("Training Performance:")
display(xgb_tuned_train_perf)
print("Testing Performance:")
display(xgb_tuned_test_perf)

Observations:¶

  • Tuned Random Forest Optimal Configuration: 5-fold cross-validation (GridSearchCV across 120 fits) selects max_depth=10, max_features=0.7, min_samples_leaf=2, and n_estimators=200.
  • Random Forest Regularization Impact: Training $R^2$ moderates from 0.9898 to 0.9581 (RMSE: 218.11, MAE: 88.58, MAPE: 3.22%), while testing $R^2$ improves from 0.9283 to 0.9315 (RMSE drops from 286.12 to 279.59, MAE: 117.16, MAPE: 4.23%). The train-to-test $R^2$ gap shrinks from 6.15% down to 2.66%.
  • Tuned XGBoost Optimal Configuration: 5-fold cross-validation (GridSearchCV across 360 fits) selects colsample_bytree=1.0, learning_rate=0.05, max_depth=5, n_estimators=200, and subsample=0.8.
  • XGBoost Optimization Impact: Training $R^2$ shifts from 0.9828 to 0.9504 (RMSE: 237.14, MAE: 96.46, MAPE: 3.67%), while testing $R^2$ rises from 0.9145 to 0.9280 (RMSE drops by 25.73 from 312.28 to 286.56, MAE drops from 138.05 to 119.58, and MAPE drops from 5.07% to 4.39%). The train-to-test $R^2$ gap contracts from 6.83% to 2.24%.

Observations:¶

  • Cross-Model Generalization Improvement: Hyperparameter tuning substantially reduces overfitting across both architectures—shrinking the train-test $R^2$ spread from 6.15% to 2.66% for Random Forest and from 6.83% to 2.24% for XGBoost.
  • Out-of-Sample Accuracy Leader: Tuned Random Forest achieves the highest testing $R^2$ (0.9315 vs. 0.9280 for Tuned XGBoost) and the lowest testing RMSE (279.59 vs. 286.56 for Tuned XGBoost), while maintaining a low test MAPE of 4.23%.
  • Final Model Selection & Serialization: Tuned Random Forest Regressor is selected as the final production model and serialized alongside the ColumnTransformer preprocessing pipeline to backend_files/superkart_model.joblib for containerized Flask API deployment.

Deployment - Backend¶

Points to note before executing the below cells¶

  • Generate a Personal Access Token
    • Make sure the token has repo scope (full control of private repositories)

  • We will deploy both the Flask backend and the Streamlit frontend as separate Docker containers inside a GitHub Codespace, and connect them using a Docker network

Flask Web Framework¶

Flask is a lightweight, flexible Python web framework used to build web applications and APIs quickly and easily.

Flask allows you to:

  • Create web routes (URLs that users can access)
  • Handle HTTP requests and responses
  • Build REST APIs to expose machine learning models or other services

In [39]:
%%writefile backend_files/app.py
import os
import joblib
import pandas as pd
from flask import Flask, request, jsonify

# Initialize the Flask application
superkart_api = Flask("SuperKart Sales Prediction API")

# Load the serialized model pipeline
model = joblib.load("superkart_model.joblib")

@superkart_api.get("/")
def home():
    return "Welcome to the SuperKart Sales Forecasting API!"

# Endpoint for online (single) inference
@superkart_api.post("/v1/predict")
def predict_sales():
    product_data = request.get_json()
    input_df = pd.DataFrame([product_data])
    prediction = model.predict(input_df).tolist()[0]
    return jsonify({"Predicted_Store_Sales": round(float(prediction), 2)})

# Endpoint for batch inference (CSV upload)
@superkart_api.post("/v1/predictbatch")
def predict_sales_batch():
    file = request.files["file"]
    input_data = pd.read_csv(file)
    predictions = [round(float(x), 2) for x in model.predict(input_data).tolist()]

    # Return dictionary mapping row IDs/indices to predicted values
    if "Product_Id" in input_data.columns:
        output_dict = dict(zip(input_data["Product_Id"], predictions))
    else:
        output_dict = {str(i): pred for i, pred in enumerate(predictions)}
    return jsonify(output_dict)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    superkart_api.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=7860, debug=False)

st.set_page_config(page_title="SuperKart Sales Forecast", layout="wide")

col1, col2 = st.columns(2)

with col1:

with col2:
    Store_Size = st.selectbox("Store Size", ["Medium", "High", "Small"])
    Store_Location_City_Type = st.selectbox("Store Location City Type", ["Tier 1", "Tier 2", "Tier 3"])
    Store_Type = st.selectbox("Store Type", ["Supermarket Type1", "Supermarket Type2", "Departmental Store", "Food Mart"])
    Store_Age_Years = st.number_input("Store Age (Years)", min_value=0, max_value=50, value=16, step=1)

payload = {

}

if st.button("Predict Store Sales", type="primary"):

        pred_val = response.json().get("Predicted_Store_Sales")
        st.success(f"Predicted Product Store Sales Total: **${pred_val:,.2f}**")
    else:

st.divider()

    else:

import json
import subprocess

# 1. Load GitHub credentials and repository details from githubconfig.json
config_path = "/content/githubconfig.json"

with open(config_path, "r") as f:
    gh_config = json.load(f)

GITHUB_USERNAME = gh_config["GITHUB_USERNAME"].strip()
GITHUB_REPO = gh_config["GITHUB_REPO"].strip()
GITHUB_EMAIL = gh_config["GITHUB_EMAIL"].strip()
GITHUB_PAT = gh_config["GITHUB_PAT"].strip()

print(f"Loaded config for GitHub user '{GITHUB_USERNAME}' -> repo '{GITHUB_REPO}'")

# 2. Create repository via GitHub API if it doesn't already exist
headers = {
    "Authorization": f"token {GITHUB_PAT}",
    "Accept": "application/vnd.github.v3+json"
}
create_resp = requests.post(
    "https://api.github.com/user/repos",
    headers=headers,
    json={"name": GITHUB_REPO, "private": False, "auto_init": False}
)
if create_resp.status_code == 201:
    print(f"Created new GitHub repository: {GITHUB_USERNAME}/{GITHUB_REPO}")
elif create_resp.status_code == 422:
    print(f"Repository {GITHUB_USERNAME}/{GITHUB_REPO} already exists. Proceeding to push files...")
else:
    print(f"GitHub API status ({create_resp.status_code}): {create_resp.text}")

# 3. Initialize Git, commit backend_files and frontend_files, and push to main
repo_url = f"https://{GITHUB_USERNAME}:{GITHUB_PAT}@github.com/{GITHUB_USERNAME}/{GITHUB_REPO}.git"

commands = [
    "git init",
    f'git config user.email "{GITHUB_EMAIL}"',
    f'git config user.name "{GITHUB_USERNAME}"',
    "git branch -M main",
    "git add backend_files/ frontend_files/",
    'git commit -m "Add SuperKart Flask backend and Streamlit frontend deployment files"',
    "git remote remove origin || true",
    f"git remote add origin {repo_url}",
    "git push -u origin main --force"
]

for cmd in commands:
    res = subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True, capture_output=True, text=True)
    if res.returncode != 0 and "commit" not in cmd:
        print(f"Warning on '{cmd.split()[0]}': {res.stderr.strip()}")

print(f"\nSuccessfully pushed backend_files/ and frontend_files/ to GitHub ({GITHUB_USERNAME}/{GITHUB_REPO})!")

Inferencing using Flask API¶

As the frontend and backend are decoupled, we can access the backend directly for predictions.

  • The decoupling ensures seamless interaction with the deployed model while leveraging the API for scalable inference.

Let's see how to interact with the deployed Flask API running inside a GitHub Codespace to perform online and batch inference from this Colab notebook.

We will:

  1. Send API requests for both online and batch inference.
  2. Process and check the model predictions.

Before running the cells below, make sure:

  • Your Codespace is running with both containers up
  • Port 7860 has been set to Public in the Codespace Ports tab
  • You have copied the forwarded URL for port 7860
  • You have also referred the document titled Guided Hands-on - Containerized Model Deployment using GitHub Codespaces provided

Online¶

Online Inference: Sending a single request to the API and receiving an immediate response. This is useful for real-time applications like recommendation systems and fraud detection.

  • This data is sent as a JSON payload in a POST request to the model endpoint.

  • The model processes the input features and returns a prediction.

Batch¶

Batch Inference: Sending multiple inputs in a single request, allowing efficient processing of large datasets. This is ideal for analyzing historical data at scale.

In [58]:
batch_dataset = pd.read_csv("Batch_Data_SuperKart.csv")

Note: The batch CSV file must contain all the feature columns expected by the model: Product_Weight, Product_Sugar_Content, Product_Allocated_Area, Product_MRP, Store_Size, Store_Location_City_Type, Store_Type, Product_Id_char, Store_Age_Years, Product_Type_Category.

In [59]:
# Prepare batch input for API request
batch_input = {
    'file': batch_dataset.to_csv(header=True, index=False).encode('utf-8')
}

This code prepares the product data as a file-like object to send in an API request (in the files parameter of requests.post).

  • batch_dataset: This is a Pandas DataFrame containing the product data loaded from a CSV file.

  • .to_csv(header=True, index=False): Converts the DataFrame into a CSV string, keeping the column headers (header=True) but excluding the index (index=False).

  • .encode('utf-8'): Encodes the CSV string into bytes (UTF-8 format), which is necessary for sending it over an HTTP request.

  • 'file': ...: Wraps the encoded CSV data in a dictionary with the key 'file', which is expected by the Flask backend.

In [60]:
# Send request to the model API for batch predictions
response = requests.post(
    model_batch_url,  # Model endpoint URL
    files=batch_input
)

This line sends a POST request to the deployed model API to perform batch sales prediction.

  • requests.post(...): This uses the requests library to make a POST request to a web server (in this case, our API endpoint for batch predictions).

  • model_batch_url: This is the URL endpoint where the batch prediction API is hosted. It should look like this:
    "https://<your-codespace-name>-7860.app.github.dev/v1/predictbatch"

  • files=batch_input: This sends the batch data file (e.g., a CSV) as part of the request using the files parameter.

  • response: This is the result of the API call and contains the response from the server, including predicted sales values.

Actionable Insights and Business Recommendations¶

1. Key Analytical & Modeling Insights¶

  • Primary Product Revenue Drivers (Product_MRP & Product_Weight):
    • Maximum Retail Price (Product_MRP) is the strongest positive linear predictor of store revenue ($r = 0.79$), spanning from 31.00 to 266.00 (mean: 147.03). Higher-priced products establish the upper revenue boundary across all store formats.
    • Product Weight (Product_Weight) exhibits a strong positive correlation with revenue ($r = 0.74$) and a moderate correlation with Product_MRP ($r = 0.53$), reflecting that bulkier family-pack and multi-unit SKUs systematically command higher retail price points and transaction totals.
  • Regional & Store Format Performance (Store_Location_City_Type, Store_Type, Store_Size):
    • Tier 1 Departmental Stores (OUT003, Medium, established 1999) and Tier 2 Supermarket Type 1 (OUT001, High, established 1987) generate the highest per-product revenue distributions, with median quarterly sales exceeding 4,000.00.
    • Tier 2 Supermarket Type 2 (OUT004, Medium, established 2009) represents the largest share of product records (53.4%, 4,676 items) and achieves moderate median sales around 3,300.00.
    • Tier 3 Food Marts (OUT002, Small, established 1998) experience a structural revenue ceiling near a median of 1,900.00, constrained by smaller physical footprints (13.1% of total records) and lower Tier 3 consumer purchasing power.
  • Shelf Space Efficiency (Product_Allocated_Area):
    • Display area ratio is right-skewed (skew = 1.13, mean 6.88%, max 29.8%) and exhibits near-zero direct linear correlation with revenue on its own. Allocating larger shelf space to low-MRP items does not independently drive higher sales totals.
  • Catalog Composition & Perishability (Product_Id_char, Product_Type_Category):
    • Inventory is dominated by Food (FD, 74.6% / 6,539 items), followed by Non-Consumables (NC, 17.3% / 1,519 items) and Drinks (DR, 8.0% / 705 items), with Low Sugar items comprising 55.7% of all SKUs.
    • Supply-chain volume is evenly split between Non-Perishables (50.5%, 4,428 items) and Perishables (49.5%, 4,335 items), led by Fruits and Vegetables (14.3%) and Snack Foods (13.1%).
  • Production Model Accuracy & Containerized Deployment:
    • Constraining tree complexity via 5-fold cross-validation (GridSearchCV) reduced the train-to-test $R^2$ generalization gap from 6.15% to 2.66% for Random Forest and from 6.83% to 2.24% for XGBoost.
    • The Tuned Random Forest Regressor (max_depth=10, max_features=0.7, min_samples_leaf=2, n_estimators=200) achieved the highest out-of-sample accuracy (Test $R^2 = 0.9315$, Adj. $R^2 = 0.9311$, RMSE = 279.59, MAPE = 4.23%) and is operationalized via a decoupled Docker network connecting the Flask REST API (/v1/predict and /v1/predictbatch) and Streamlit UI.

2. Actionable Business Recommendations¶

  • Tailor Regional Assortment & Pricing by City Tier:
    • Tier 1 (Departmental Store) & High-Footprint Tier 2 (Supermarket Type 1): Expand premium and higher-MRP assortments (165.00–266.00 range) alongside larger weight packs (Product_Weight > 14.0), as affluent urban demographics and larger store footprints consistently convert high-ticket items into 4,000+ per-SKU revenue.
    • Tier 3 (Food Mart): Restrict high-MRP slow movers and curate high-velocity, mid-to-low MRP essentials (80.00–145.00 range) in compact package weights to maximize revenue per square foot within Small store formats.
  • Reallocate Promotional Shelf Space (Product_Allocated_Area) Based on Margin Contribution:
    • Audit SKUs currently occupying top-quartile display area (>9.6% allocated area) that generate below-median sales (<3,452.34).
